1	<!-- What Pavol has decided, holds or already knows, as it stands now: each position in plain words, what we do and why, under a bold title that is its handle; a quote only where his words are the position itself. Timeless: no dates, no provenance, no account of how a position was reached. That record is `POSITIONS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim with what became of it. A position he has replaced is gone from here and the later one stands; a decision not yet built keeps the detail the coming work needs. A worker or a coordinator may add an entry with a date or a quote in it; the next consolidation compiles that out into the history and leaves the position. Standing directives about how we work are in `explorations/protocol.md`, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. Read whole at session start, so that none of it is re-asked or re-explained. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
8	- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
9	- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
10	- **The APL side quest is closed.** It was a curiosity, then a ladder to learn APL, then native code (not an interpreter in an interpreter) with microGPT as its target; its remaining ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued.
11	- **The 2D notation is a gimmick.** Fortify's mathematical rendering is "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, while the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress; no work on it unless he asks.
12	- **The type checker on interpreter programs.** He wants the checker, which runs only on the compile path, usable on interpreter programs, and considers it low-hanging fruit. It comes after the switch-over, when walk also takes the static coercions the checker inserts (the entry on walk's choice of coercions).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- **The project's end.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
17	- **Boxed numerics.** The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here". The first measurement's scalar loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator); the fairer test he asked for agreed with him (FACTS § Execution model). The storage is his decision below; unboxed arithmetic is phase 6 of the plan.
18	- **Hsu's critique** of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
19	- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.
20	
21	## Decisions on record
22	
23	### The standard and the sources
24	
25	- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
26	- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 by Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
27	- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
28	- **Fleshing out the standard library** is a very important task: first the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch (done by the flattening), then the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them; into the standard library itself, not a tree of our own.
29	- **Interpreter performance is irrelevant.** "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed, and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled. The two microGPT programs never run in the gate ("those are too long running to be tests"); the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
30	- **The microGPT walk check is quick.** Under walk, the check of the model after a batch proves that its mathematics still works and that the library changes did not break it: about two forward-and-backward passes against the reference values, under one minute, never a full run of every check; the full check programs run only when asked. "it needs to run under a minute, okay? That's the goal. Otherwise, it's useless waste of time."
31	- **Development-loop performance is a first-class concern.** When an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
32	- **The territory map** (`coordinator/map/`) is the map down to where the design intent is written, papers as well as the specification; he wanted it before unsealing. The maps exist so that nothing on record is rediscovered; the boot order is followed as written, `INDEX.md` included.
33	- **The plan** (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) is six phases, approved with its workers: 1, the wrapping operators, the specification rung without the number chapters and the run-time size rung; 2, the flattening, the number chapters and the overflow natives; 3, the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code-generation holes; 6, microGPT fast. Phases 1 and 2 are landed. His answers come in the plan's order; the re-approval rows and the other off-path items are parked until relevant; row 41 joins the switch-over's design.
34	
35	### The one library and the compiled checker
36	
37	- **The library route.** "we need to unify this. into single library"; "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it." One library, the interpreter's (`FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin`), becomes the library the compiler checks; no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`); the prelude-name rungs of the ladder stopped, code-generator rungs continue; the three prelude files are deleted at the switch-over and their tests kept. How the checker is brought to accept the library is a plan put to him step by step, not a decision to re-ask.
38	- **The compiler prelude's leftovers go at the switch-over.** The compiler-prelude block for `Maybe` stands as landed, its tests kept, its lines gone then; the guard `if other = -1 then 0` in the two compiled `REM` bodies (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:601`, `:686`) stays and goes with the prelude; the prelude's reversed spellings of the wrapping and saturating operators (row 348) are respelled then, in 10 compiled test files; `ZZ64`'s compiled shift declaration (row 381) closes when the compiled path reads this library; the specification's `shift` (row 383) reaches the compiled path then, `compiler_tests/XXXShiftDeclRungI.test` promoted and `shift` a reserved name on the compiled path from then on, the switch-over batch measuring which compiler tests bind it.
39	- **The checker count is measured, never red.** The checker-count stage stays in every gate, reported and never red on its own; the full distance measurement (all apis and components) is a report-only stage of the phase-3 gates, whose job is driving it down.
40	- **Sizes.** The checker checks `nat` and `int` parameters (built). A size left unknown after inference is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing otherwise ("the middle is a clear winner"); how the checker represents an unknown size was not his to decide. Deleting the dead sizes (E3, 25 api declarations) is shown to him as a diff with the switch-over's design, with row 41. Every static argument counts in the exclusion rule except operator arguments ("sizes count"); booleans follow once the checker supports boolean parameters (row 406). A size the call cannot fix is an error at that call, also inside overload sets: when the arm the rules would pick has a size the call cannot fix, the call is refused with the same "could not infer" error instead of the arm being dropped (row 400 closed). A `nat` parameter is an `NN32` value and an `int` parameter a `ZZ32` (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:82-90`); a larger one is refused; the array design refuses a JVM array length over 2^31-1 where it makes storage ("that's not even a question"). A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does (row 485); sizes as `NN32` and ranges as `ZZ32` are consistent, since array lengths and indices are Java `int`, a size is never negative and ranges count through negatives. All built.

5	## Execution model
6	
7	- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:97-129`).
8	- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
9	- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:453-458` calls `useCompilerLibraries()`; row 69). The checker on interpreter programs comes after the switch-over (POSITIONS, "The type checker on interpreter programs.").
10	- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the run-time class `FRR64`, so a compiled loop over `RR64` holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (`repo-internals.md:129`; the bytecode quoted in `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 4). An array is a library object read and written through `get` and `put` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1417`, `:1468`), not a `double[]`.
11	- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost: in Java models of the program's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4). No microGPT-shaped kernel compiles: the compiler prelude has no array type, and `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` are undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305). No array type goes into the compiler prelude; the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (POSITIONS, "The library route."). A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (row 304).
12	- With rows 302 and 303 fixed (the next two entries), the compiled scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` runs in 0.74 s, against 13.06 s on the tree before them, a pair timed in one session (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Two costs that the boxing probe named in that loop are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 5). One is the `for` lowered to the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, a recursive binary subdivision over boxed indices with a closure call per element (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:373-381`). The other is the representational rest, which unboxed doubles would attack: the transacted volatile cell, four allocations per iteration, the interface hop to the native wrapper and the `checkcast`s.
13	- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
14	- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
15	- The benchmark numbers on record, `bench1t` 9.3441 s and `bench1h` 6.0732 s (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`, `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`), are one session's: the same unmodified tree timed 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s in another (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions; only a before-and-after pair taken in one session measures a difference.
16	- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars when it changes the implementation, and only then: it deletes the caches whole when the sources or the build differ from what the last successful build left ("**`ant compileAll` deletes the caches folder, the linker's untracked `global.map` with it, when the implementation changed, and keeps it otherwise**" under The harness and the gate), and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:172-185` restores the jars in about two minutes. Nothing else clears `bytecode_cache/`: with the caches kept through a rebuilt compiler, the five library jars survive and a compiled program runs (`coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 2).
17	- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
18	- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); a size is in the stamped class's name (`pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, `perf-probes/nat/java.md` § 1; `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`), and its descriptor in a stamped class is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics).
19	- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`Specification/basic/expressions/tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool. No program under `explorations/` writes `spawn` or `also`.
20	- Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are instantiated at run time with numeric values (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:97`). The compiled checker checks them ("The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" under The checker and the one library), and a sized program loads and runs compiled ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics). Sizes check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them. Under walk, a `nat` parameter does not unify with a run-time-built array, while a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", a `ProgramError` that no `catch` takes (row 254). Row 83, a `nat`-generic function that mis-unifies on its second instantiation through an api, is contested and has no reproducer.
21	- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** The Working Draft's `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`) stops on both paths with a syntax error at `excludes`, because the grammar gives an object no `excludes` clause (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:84-86`; `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, `fortress compile` and `fortress walk` give the same single error, `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md`, "Why the specification cannot simply be transcribed"). The specification keeps the declaration marked "Not allowed" and gives instantiation exclusion and the missing `excludes` clause as the reasons (`Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:58-73`); the parametric spelling stands (POSITIONS, "`Maybe`'s empty case").
22	- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (`compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`; row 320). Both paths assume an api and its implementing component share a name: `fortress link` and `walk` print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path", and the compiled run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The assumption is `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`'s fallback to the api's own name (`linker/Linker.java:72-76`); only `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` register another. The specification resolves an imported api to a component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex:33-35`), and the team reserved the codegen half in `CodeGen.java:417-450`, `:1859`, `:6660-6666`. Gated as an expected failure by `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test`. The workaround is to name the api after its component (row 320).
23	- **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it** (`compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1; ledger row 359). `createSpan` (`parser/Fortress.rats:145-157`) trims back over space characters only; a declaration ending in `end` is unaffected.
